conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived.  
We’ll use a short, well-studied form called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can show up after childbirth.  
Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell us someone is in immediate danger. This is a judgment-free space; many new mothers find it a relief to talk openly.  
I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

To start:  
Over the past seven days, overall have you been able to enjoy things, or has enjoyment felt hard to come by?

Honestly, most things feel kind of… flat. I still smile when the baby grips my finger, but even the little stuff I used to like—watching a show, texting friends—feels more like a chore than a break. I wouldn’t say I’ve lost all joy, it’s just harder to reach and doesn’t last long.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh, especially when my partner pulls those silly faces to calm the baby, but it feels kind of forced or tired—like I’m laughing because I know it’s funny, not because it bubbles up naturally. The funny side of life hasn’t disappeared, it’s just muted.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I’ll make plans—like taking the baby to the park or meeting a friend for coffee—because I think I *should* look forward to them, but when the time comes I feel kind of numb and would rather stay home. It worries me that even small outings feel like a chore rather than something I actually want to do.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like, if the baby won’t settle at night, my mind jumps to “I must be doing something wrong” or “I’m not soothing him right.” I know rationally babies cry, but I still catch myself feeling it’s my fault, especially when I’m already tired.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few times a day I’ll suddenly feel on-edge—heart racing, scanning the room—without anything specific happening. I’ll check if the baby’s breathing in the bassinet or worry the bottle temp is wrong, even when everything seems fine. It’s not constant, but it pops up enough that I notice it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, it’s happened twice this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my heart’s racing, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen—even though the baby’s asleep and the house is quiet. It passes after a few minutes, but those minutes feel like I’m losing control.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s not that any one thing is huge—just the combo of feeding, changing, trying to sleep, and then the laundry pile or a text I forgot to answer. I’ll stand in the kitchen feeling like I’m drowning in tiny tasks and think, “I can’t keep up,” even though I know they’re small.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t call it “so unhappy,” more like my mind won’t shut off. After the last night feeding, I lie there running through did-I-sterilize-the-pump-parts, is-he-breathing, will-I-ever-feel-normal-again… and by the time I drift off, it’s almost time for the next feed. It’s happened maybe four nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like a heaviness sits on me for a couple of hours a day—but it lifts here and there when the baby smiles or my partner makes dinner. So, yes, I’ve been sad, but it’s not all day, every day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I teared up once yesterday when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt useless, but actual crying has been rare—maybe once in the past week. Mostly it’s just that tight-throat feeling without the tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that since your baby arrived the sparkle has faded from everyday moments-activities you used to enjoy now feel flat or like chores, and a persistent heaviness settles over you for parts of each day. You still find little lifts when your baby grips your finger or your partner makes you laugh, yet the pleasure is muted and short-lived. Most days you feel swamped by ordinary tasks, catch yourself unfairly blaming you when the baby fusses, and notice sudden waves of anxiety or even panic that come out of nowhere. Sleep is hard because your mind races with worries about sterilised parts, breathing checks, and "will I ever feel normal again?" You've been sad but not hopeless, teary only once, and you've never thought of harming yourself-yet you're aware something isn't right and you want help feeling like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports feeling numb, avoiding outings, and experiencing no real enjoyment or anticipation despite trying to plan things, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame occurs "some of the time" with specific examples matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes noticeable, recurrent episodes of unexplained anxiety multiple times daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm with multiple small tasks, indicating impaired coping "most days" but not absolute inability to function, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent sleep-disrupting rumination 4/7 nights, aligning with "sometimes" though she avoids the word "unhappy."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily sadness for a couple of hours, which closely aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 17 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive episode with peripartum onset</med>. DSM-5 criteria are met through: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), depressed mood most days, inappropriate guilt, anxiety/panic, and reduced sleep. Answers map to item scores: Q2 (anhedonia) 3, Q8 (sadness) 2, Q3 (self-blame) 2, Q4 & Q5 (anxiety/panic) 2 each, Q7 (sleep) 2, Q6 (coping) 2. Q10 score 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent review with your <med>GP</med>, <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health team</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss whether an <med>antidepressant</med> is appropriate while breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 30-min pleasant activity you once enjoyed (music, short walk, gentle yoga) to counter <sym>anhedonia</sym>
4. Set a simple wind-down routine: low lighting, screen-off 30 min before bed, write tomorrow's to-do list to quiet racing thoughts
5. Invite your partner or a friend to handle one night feed so you can get a 4-5 h stretch of sleep; adequate rest is the fastest way to lower <sym>anxiety</sym>
6. Keep the baby-safe environment you already have (smoke alarm, clear floors) and consider a bedside cot for easier night settling
7. Schedule a 2-week follow-up EPDS to monitor progress; if thoughts of self-harm develop, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, partner present, infant 2–3 wks old.

Presenting Symptoms / Concerns  
– Anhedonia: marked reduction in spontaneous enjoyment; activities planned “because I should” feel “numb”  
– Low mood: daily “heaviness” several hrs, situational lift when baby smiles  
– Excessive guilt/self-blame around infant care (“I must be doing something wrong”)  
– Recurrent intrusive worries (baby breathing, bottle temp) with autonomic arousal  
– Two discrete panic attacks this wk (chest tightness, racing heart, fear of catastrophe)  
– Persistent “on-edge” state multiple × daily  
– Sleep disruption secondary to mental hyper-arousal (racing thoughts about chores, infant safety) ~4 nights/wk  
– Subjective sense of being “drowned” by routine tasks most days

Observed Patterns  
– Symptoms began after delivery, worsening over past 1–2 wks  
– Fluctuating course: symptoms partially remit with partner support or infant positive cues  
– No anhedonia or sadness is absolute (still laughs with partner, smiles at baby)  
– No crying spells; only one episode of tearing up  
– No self-harm, suicidal, or infanticidal ideation (explicitly denied)

Screening Significance  
Meets subthreshold to mild criteria for:  
1. Major depressive episode with peripartum onset (anhedonia, low mood, guilt, sleep disturbance)  
2. Anxiety features consistent with postpartum generalized / panic spectrum

Risk Factors  
– Primiparity, sleep deprivation, cognitive self-blame style, episodic panic  
– Protective: strong partner support, good insight, no prior MH history per self-report, denies substance use, denies self-harm

Safety  
– Active suicidal/homicidal ideation: NONE elicited (documented denial Q10)  
– No plan, intent, or means reported

Overall Screening Impression  
Moderate postpartum mood and anxiety symptoms causing functional impairment; warrants further clinical evaluation, psychoeducation, supportive counseling, and safety-planning.
